6 Modelling and Visualising Accessibility using Hansen Method
The code chunk below uses ac() to compute the Hansen’s accessibility and saves the output in a data frame by using data.frame().

acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            power = 0.5,
                            family = "Hansen"))


# Create a list to store all results
hansen_results <- list()

# Calculate accessibility for each power value
power_values <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5)

for (power_val in power_values) {
  acc_temp <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            power = power_val,
                            family = "Hansen"))
  colnames(acc_temp) <- paste0("accHansen_power", power_val)
  hansen_results[[as.character(power_val)]] <- acc_temp
}

# Combine all results
acc_Hansen_all <- bind_cols(hansen_results)

# For your existing workflow, keep one version (e.g., power = 2)
acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            power = 2,
                            family = "Hansen"))

6.1 Visualising Hansen’s Accessibility

6.1.1 Extracting Map Extend
First, we extract the extent of the hexagon sf layer using st_bbox() of sf package.

mapex <- st_bbox(hexagons)

Next, we create a choropleth map with the tmap package to visualise eldercare service accessibility across Singapore.

tm_shape(hexagon_Hansen,
         bbox = mapex) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "accHansen", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: Hansen method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)









# Create maps for all power values for comparison
for (power_val in power_values) {
  col_name <- paste0("accHansen_power", power_val)
  temp_hexagon <- bind_cols(hexagons, hansen_results[[as.character(power_val)]])
  
  print(
    tm_shape(temp_hexagon,
             bbox = mapex) + 
      tm_polygons(fill = col_name, 
                  fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                    style = "quantile",
                    n = 10,
                    values = "brewer.blues")) +
      tm_shape(eldercare) +
      tm_dots(size = 0.3,
              fill = "red",
              col = "black") +
      tm_title(paste("Hansen Accessibility - Power =", power_val)) +
      tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
      tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
      tm_scalebar() +
      tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
  )
}





































Power = 0.5 Weak distance decay - accessibility spreads widely across Singapore, creating a smooth pattern with minimal variation between near and far locations.
Power = 1.0 Moderate decay - clearer concentration around facilities emerges, but surrounding areas still maintain reasonable accessibility with visible gradients.
Power = 1.5 Strong decay - steep accessibility drop-off creates distinct service zones around each facility, highlighting spatial inequality between central and peripheral areas.
Power = 2.0 Very strong decay - accessibility highly localized immediately around facilities, with large regions showing near-zero access and sharp peaks at facility locations.
Power = 2.5 Extreme decay - accessibility limited to immediate facility vicinity, vast majority of Singapore shows minimal access, emphasizing critical importance of proximity.
As the power parameter increases, accessibility becomes increasingly concentrated around eldercare facilities due to stronger distance decay. Lower powers (0.5-1.0) create more equitable but potentially overestimated accessibility, while higher powers (1.5-2.5) produce highly localized patterns that better reflect distance friction but may underestimate access for intermediate distances. The choice of power value represents a trade-off between modeling realistic distance barriers and capturing broader spatial accessibility patterns.

title: Take home Exercise 3 : Predictive Modelling of HDB Resale Prices with Geographically Weighted Methods
text: This study develops predictive models for HDB 4-room resale prices in Singapore using geographically weighted methods. We implement and compare multiple modelling approaches including Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR), Random Forest, and Geographically Weighted Random Forest (GRF). The analysis leverages both structural attributes and locational factors to capture the complex spatial patterns in Singapore’s public housing market and approaches to identify the most accurate predictive model for housing prices from July to September 2025 based on data from July 2024 to June 2025.

# Improved geocoding function with better error handling
geocode_improved <- function(block, streetname) {
  base_url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"
  address <- paste(block, streetname, sep = " ")
  query <- list("searchVal" = address, 
                "returnGeom" = "Y",

                "pageNum" = "1")
  
  tryCatch({
    res <- GET(base_url, query = query)
    restext <- content(res, as="text", encoding = "UTF-8")
    
    output <- fromJSON(restext)
    
    if (!is.null(output$found) && output$found > 0) {
      # Extract first result coordinates as numeric

      lon <- as.numeric(output$results$LONGITUDE[1])
      return(list(LATITUDE = lat, LONGITUDE = lon))
    } else {
      return(list(LATITUDE = NA, LONGITUDE = NA))
    }
  }, error = function(e) {
    return(list(LATITUDE = NA, LONGITUDE = NA))

4 Data Cleaning and Feature Engineering

clean_street_names <- function(data) {
  data %>%
    mutate(street_name = gsub("ST\\.", "SAINT", street_name))
}

engineer_features <- function(data) {
  data %>%
    mutate(
      # Convert storey range to ordinal scale
      storey_order = case_when(
        storey_range == "01 TO 03" ~ 1,
        storey_range == "04 TO 06" ~ 2,
        storey_range == "07 TO 09" ~ 3,
        storey_range == "10 TO 12" ~ 4,
        storey_range == "13 TO 15" ~ 5,
        storey_range == "16 TO 18" ~ 6,
        storey_range == "19 TO 21" ~ 7,
        storey_range == "22 TO 24" ~ 8,
        storey_range == "25 TO 27" ~ 9,
        storey_range == "28 TO 30" ~ 10,
        storey_range == "31 TO 33" ~ 11,
        storey_range == "34 TO 36" ~ 12,
        storey_range == "37 TO 39" ~ 13,
        storey_range == "40 TO 42" ~ 14,
        TRUE ~ 7  # Default for unknown ranges
      ),
      # Calculate remaining lease in months
      lease_commence_year = as.numeric(lease_commence_date),
      current_year = 2025,
      flat_age = current_year - lease_commence_year,
      remaining_lease_years = 99 - flat_age,
      remaining_lease_mths = remaining_lease_years * 12
    ) %>%
    select(-lease_commence_year, -current_year, -flat_age, -remaining_lease_years)
}

# Apply cleaning and feature engineering
train_clean <- train_raw %>% clean_street_names() %>% engineer_features()
test_clean <- test_raw %>% clean_street_names() %>% engineer_features()

Feature engineering transforms categorical variables (storey_range) into ordinal numeric variables and calculates remaining lease in months, which are more suitable for regression models.

text:
Market area analysis (also known as Trade Area Analysis) is the process of defining and studying the geographical area from which a business draws its customers. It involves analyzing data on consumer demographics, spending habits, and competitors to understand market viability, identify opportunities, and inform decisions about location, marketing, and expansion. It often combines empirical observation, like customer spotting, with mathematical models to identify market segments and understand customer behavior.
Huff model is a geospatial analysis method commonly used in market area analysis to predict the probability that a consumer from a specific area will patronize a particular store, based on the store’s attractiveness and distance relative to competitors. It calculates a store’s market share by considering factors like size or sales for attractiveness and distance or travel time, with the probability decreasing as distance or competition increases. This tool helps businesses assess potential revenue, define trade areas, and make informed decisions about site selection

title: Take home Exercise 3 : Predictive Modelling of HDB Resale Prices with Geographically Weighted Methods
text:
2 Background
Singapore’s public housing market exhibits unique spatial characteristics due to the island’s planned urban development and varying estate maturity. Traditional global regression models often fail to capture local variations in housing price determinants. This study addresses spatial heterogeneity by implementing geographically weighted approaches that allow relationships between price drivers to vary across different neighbourhoods, providing more accurate predictions and deeper insights into local market dynamics.

# Geocode primary schools using OneMap API
cat("Geocoding primary schools...\n")

Geocoding primary schools...

geocode_school <- function(postal_code) {
  base_url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"
  query <- list("searchVal" = postal_code,
                "returnGeom" = "Y",
                "getAddrDetails" = "N",
                "pageNum" = "1")
  
  tryCatch({
    res <- GET(base_url, query = query, timeout(10))
    if (status_code(res) == 200) {
      content_data <- content(res, as = "parsed")
      if (!is.null(content_data$found) && content_data$found > 0) {
        first_result <- content_data$results[[1]]
        return(list(
          LATITUDE = as.numeric(first_result$LATITUDE),
          LONGITUDE = as.numeric(first_result$LONGITUDE),
          status = "success"
        ))
      }
    }
    return(list(LATITUDE = NA, LONGITUDE = NA, status = "no_results"))
  }, error = function(e) {
    return(list(LATITUDE = NA, LONGITUDE = NA, status = "error"))
  })
}
